title: What training and qualifications does the Maritime Labour Convention require before a seafarer can work on a ship?
description: MLC, 2006 Regulation 1.3 on seafarer training and qualifications, cook and medical training standards, and ratification in five markets, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: Regulation 1.3 of the International Labour Organization's Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 says seafarers shall not work on a ship unless they are trained or certified as competent or otherwise qualified for their duties, and have completed training for personal safety on board. Training and certification under IMO instruments such as STCW counts as meeting both requirements. Australia, Japan and Portugal have ratified the Convention; the United States and the United Arab Emirates have not.
keyTakeaways: The MLC, 2006 was adopted on February 23, 2006, entered into force on August 20, 2013, and had 113 ratifications as at November 2026.
Regulation 1.3 has no separate Code standard: it relies on IMO instruments, so STCW training and certification is deemed to satisfy it.
Specific training duties sit elsewhere in the Code, including ships' cooks (Standard A3.2) and medical first aid and medical care training to STCW standards (Standard A4.1).
Australia ratified on December 21, 2011, Japan on August 5, 2013 and Portugal on May 12, 2016; the United States and the UAE do not appear on the ILO ratification list.
The 2025 amendments, which add shipboard violence and harassment duties and port personnel training on shore leave, are expected to enter into force on December 23, 2027.
jurisdiction: International (ILO), with ratification status for Australia, Portugal, Japan, the United States and the United Arab Emirates
regulator: International Labour Organization (ILO); flag State and port State maritime authorities in ratifying countries
appliesTo: Shipowners and operators of ships flying the flag of a ratifying State
Seafarers, meaning any person employed, engaged or working in any capacity on board a ship to which the Convention applies
Seafarers designated to provide medical first aid or in charge of medical care on board

sections.heading: What is the Maritime Labour Convention, 2006?

blocks.text: It is the ILO treaty that sets seafarers' minimum working and living conditions in a single instrument. According to the [ILO](https://www.ilo.org/international-labour-standards/maritime-labour-convention-2006), it was adopted by the 94th (Maritime) Session of the International Labour Conference on February 23, 2006 and revises and consolidates 37 earlier conventions and related recommendations. It entered into force on August 20, 2013.

The Convention has three layers: Articles, Regulations and a Code. The Code has mandatory Standards (Part A) and non-mandatory Guidelines (Part B). The ILO reports that the Code was amended in 2014, 2016, 2018, 2022 and 2025, and that ratifications represent 96.6 percent of world gross shipping tonnage.

For training managers, the Convention matters in two ways. It sets a baseline condition of employment (no untrained seafarer works on board), and it is enforced through flag State certification and port State inspection in ratifying countries, so gaps can lead to deficiencies on a ship far from its home port.

Regulation 1.3, "Training and qualifications", has the stated purpose "to ensure that seafarers are trained or qualified to carry out their duties on board ship". Its four paragraphs, from the ILO's [consolidated text including the 2022 amendments](https://www.ilo.org/sites/default/files/2024-10/NORMES_MLC%20Amendments-EN_2022_Web_1.pdf), are:

items: Seafarers shall not work on a ship unless they are trained or certified as competent or otherwise qualified to perform their duties.
Seafarers shall not be permitted to work on a ship unless they have successfully completed training for personal safety on board ship.
Training and certification in accordance with the mandatory instruments adopted by the International Maritime Organization shall be considered as meeting the requirements of paragraphs 1 and 2.

A Member bound by the Certification of Able Seamen Convention, 1946 (No. 74) when it ratified had to continue those obligations until IMO provisions covering the subject were in force or five years after the MLC entered into force, whichever was earlier.

blocks.text: Unusually for the MLC, there is no Standard A1.3 or Guideline B1.3. Paragraph 3 hands the technical content to IMO, which in practice means the [STCW Convention](/regulations/stcw-seafarer-training-requirements). Paragraph 2 also reaches people STCW may not: the MLC's definition of seafarer covers anyone working on board in any capacity, so hotel staff on a passenger ship need personal safety training too.

sections.heading: Which other MLC provisions impose training duties?

blocks.text: Several Code standards outside Regulation 1.3 set specific training requirements that a crew training plan must cover.

items: **Ships' cooks (Regulation 3.2 and Standard A3.2).** Shipowners must ensure that seafarers engaged as ships' cooks are trained, qualified and found competent. The requirement includes completing a training course approved or recognized by the competent authority covering practical cookery, food and personal hygiene, food storage, stock control, and environmental protection and catering health and safety. On ships with a prescribed manning of less than ten that need not carry a fully qualified cook, anyone processing food in the galley must be trained or instructed in food and personal hygiene and the handling and storage of food. A dispensation for a non-fully qualified cook may not exceed one month or run beyond the next convenient port of call.
**Catering staff (Standard A3.2, paragraph 2(c)).** Catering staff shall be properly trained or instructed for their positions.

**Medical care (Standard A4.1).** Ships carrying 100 or more persons on international voyages of more than three days must carry a qualified medical doctor. Ships without a doctor must have at least one seafarer in charge of medical care or competent to provide medical first aid, and that person must have completed medical care or medical first aid training that meets STCW requirements.

**Young seafarers (Standard A1.1).** Night work for seafarers under 18 is prohibited, with a narrow exception where effective training under established programs and schedules would otherwise be impaired.

blocks.text: Because the cook and medical duties are written as Standards, they are mandatory for ratifying States, which then turn them into national rules. A crewing manager should therefore treat them as separate rows in the [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix), not as part of general STCW compliance.

sections.heading: Which of the five markets have ratified the MLC?

blocks.text: Three have. The ILO's NORMLEX ratification list for the MLC, 2006 ([archived copy, September 24, 2026](https://web.archive.org/web/20260924142911/https://normlex.ilo.org/dyn/nrmlx_en/f?p=NORMLEXPUB:11300:0::NO::P11300_INSTRUMENT_ID:312331)) shows 113 ratifications and none denounced. NORMLEX itself sits behind an automated browser check, so the status below was read from that archived copy and matches the 113 ratifications the ILO's MLC page reports.

blocks.text: Non-ratification does not take a fleet outside the Convention's reach. Under Article V(4), a covered ship may be inspected by a Member other than the flag State while in one of its ports, and Article V(7) requires ratifying States to ensure that ships flying the flag of a non-ratifying State "do not receive more favourable treatment" than ships of ratifying States.

sections.heading: Which MLC amendments are in force, and which are pending?

blocks.text: According to the NORMLEX record, the 2014 amendments entered into force on January 18, 2017, the 2016 amendments on January 8, 2019, the 2018 amendments on December 26, 2020 and the 2022 amendments on December 23, 2024. The 2025 amendments were not in force as at November 2026; their expected date of entry into force is December 23, 2027.

The [2025 amendments](https://www.ilo.org/sites/default/files/2025-06/ILC113-Instruments-%5BRELMEETINGS-250605-001%5D-Web-EN.pdf), adopted at the 113th International Labour Conference, include several training-relevant changes:

items: A new Standard A4.3 paragraph 1(e) on prevention and elimination of shipboard violence and harassment, including sexual harassment, bullying and sexual assault, and new paragraphs requiring shipowners to adopt policies and measures and requiring seafarers to comply with them.
A new Guideline B2.4.5 saying personnel in ports and terminals should receive appropriate information and training on seafarers' rights, including the right to shore leave.
An updated Guideline B4.1.1 basing medical training on the latest International Medical Guide for Seafarers and Fishers and related guides.

blocks.text: Operators should plan now: harassment prevention training aligned with the [positive duty approach](/regulations/positive-duty-sexual-harassment-training) many onshore regimes already take is likely to become an inspection point once the amendments apply. Track the change using a process such as [how to update training when regulations change](/guides/how-to-update-training-when-regulations-change).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry links each MLC Standard to the flag State rule that implements it and to the STCW competence that discharges it, so a single crew training record can show both the IMO and the ILO basis for a qualification. Pending amendments such as the 2025 harassment provisions are held with their expected commencement date so training can be built before they apply.

faqs.q: Does an STCW certificate satisfy MLC Regulation 1.3?
faqs.a: Yes. Paragraph 3 of Regulation 1.3 says training and certification in accordance with the mandatory instruments adopted by the IMO shall be considered as meeting the requirements of paragraphs 1 and 2. STCW is the main such instrument. Separate MLC standards still apply to cooks and medical care.

faqs.q: Do hotel and catering staff on cruise ships need personal safety training under the MLC?
faqs.a: Yes. The MLC defines a seafarer as any person employed, engaged or working in any capacity on board a covered ship, and Regulation 1.3 paragraph 2 says seafarers shall not be permitted to work unless they have completed training for personal safety on board.

faqs.q: Has the United States ratified the Maritime Labour Convention?
faqs.a: No. The United States does not appear on the ILO's list of 113 ratifications as at November 2026, and neither does the United Arab Emirates. Ships of non-ratifying flags can still be inspected against the Convention when they call at ports of ratifying States.

faqs.q: When do the 2025 MLC amendments on violence and harassment apply?
faqs.a: They were not in force as at November 2026. The ILO's NORMLEX record gives an expected entry into force date of December 23, 2027, after a formal disagreement period ending June 23, 2027.
